title: Agents' Last Exam: Benchmarking Agents on Real Economic Work
hook: Frontier agents ace academic benchmarks but flop on real jobs — Agents' Last Exam scores them on 1,000+ economically valuable workflows, where the hardest tier sees just a 2.6% pass rate.
key_points: Argues the gap between benchmark scores and real deployment is itself an evaluation problem: benchmarks rarely test sustained, economically valuable workflows.
Built with 250+ industry experts, ALE tests agents on long-horizon, real-world tasks with verifiable outcomes.
Tasks map to the U.S. O*NET/SOC occupational taxonomy: 55 subfields across 13 industry clusters, 1,000+ tasks.
On the hardest tier, mainstream agent harnesses average just a 2.6% full pass rate — far from saturated.
content_html: AI systems post strong numbers on a wide range of benchmarks, yet those gains haven't translated into economically meaningful deployment across many professional fields. The authors argue this is largely an evaluation problem: widely used benchmarks don't sustainedly measure performance on real, economically valuable workflows.
extra_html:
The benchmark

Agents' Last Exam (ALE) evaluates AI agents on long-horizon, economically valuable, real-world tasks with verifiable outcomes. Developed with 250+ industry experts, it covers non-physical industries defined against the U.S. federal occupational taxonomy (O*NET / SOC 2018), organized into 55 subfields grouped into 13 industry clusters spanning more than 1,000 tasks. Crucially, the hardest tier is far from saturated: across mainstream harness and backbone configurations, the average full pass rate is just 2.6%.

Why it matters

ALE is pitched as a living benchmark — its task pool grows as new workflows and industries are onboarded — and as an instrument, not just a leaderboard. The goal is to close the gap between benchmark success and GDP-relevant impact, giving a more honest picture of where agents stand on the work people actually get paid to do.
